title: Drugs, Targets & Receptor Families
summary: What a drug is, how drugs are named and classified, and the major molecular targets they act on.

lessons.title: What Is a Drug? Names, Classes and Targets

levels.kid:
A drug is a special chemical that changes how your body works. Most drugs work like a key. Your cells have tiny locks on them. When the right key fits the right lock, something happens: a pain signal gets quieter, or a germ gets stopped.

Every drug has more than one name. The **generic name** is its real name, like a person's full name. The **brand name** is the name a company puts on the box, like a nickname.

Doctors group drugs into families. Drugs in the same family usually work in the same way, and their names often end in the same letters. That makes them easier to remember!
levels.hs:
A **drug** is any chemical that changes how the body works by interacting with a specific molecule inside it. That molecule is the drug's **target**. Most targets are proteins: receptors, enzymes, ion channels and transporters. A molecule that binds to a target is called a **ligand**.

Drugs have three kinds of names:
- **Chemical name**: describes the exact structure. Very long and almost never used in clinics.
- **Generic name**: the official name, used worldwide (ibuprofen).
- **Brand name**: the company's trademark (Advil). One generic drug can have many brand names.

Generic names often share a **stem** that tells you the class. Drugs ending in -olol (metoprolol) are beta blockers. Drugs ending in -pril (lisinopril) are ACE inhibitors. Drugs ending in -statin lower cholesterol, and drugs ending in -mab are monoclonal antibodies.

Drugs can be classified by **mechanism** (what they do to the target), by **therapeutic use** (what disease they treat), or by **chemical structure**. Mechanism is the most useful, because drugs that hit the same target usually share both benefits and side effects.
levels.college:
Pharmacology studies how chemicals interact with living systems. A **drug** is a chemical that alters physiological function through interaction with a molecular target. It can be **exogenous** (a xenobiotic) or a synthetic version of an **endogenous** molecule, such as insulin or epinephrine.

**Nomenclature.** Each drug has a chemical (IUPAC) name, a nonproprietary name (INN internationally, USAN in the US), and one or more proprietary (brand) names. Nonproprietary names are built from stems assigned by the WHO: -olol (β-adrenoceptor antagonists), -pril (ACE inhibitors), -sartan (angiotensin II receptor blockers), -azepam (benzodiazepines), -tinib (tyrosine kinase inhibitors), and -mab (monoclonal antibodies).

**Pharmacokinetics vs pharmacodynamics.** Pharmacokinetics (PK) is what the body does to the drug: absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion. Pharmacodynamics (PD) is what the drug does to the body: binding, signaling and effect.

**Target classes.** Most drugs act on proteins:
- **Receptors** (ligand-gated ion channels, GPCRs, enzyme-linked receptors, nuclear receptors)
- **Enzymes** (COX, ACE, HMG-CoA reductase)
- **Ion channels** (voltage-gated Na+ and Ca2+ channels)
- **Transporters** (SERT, Na+/K+-ATPase, NKCC2)

Some drugs act on nucleic acids (alkylating agents), on structural proteins (tubulin), or on targets that exist only in microbes (bacterial ribosomes). A few drugs need no target protein at all: antacids neutralize acid chemically, and mannitol works by osmosis.

**Selectivity** is relative. Every drug binds more than one target at high enough concentrations, which is why "selective" always means "selective within a concentration range".
levels.phd:
A pharmacological agent is best defined operationally: a molecule whose binding to a macromolecular target, or whose physicochemical action, produces a measurable change in a biological system. The **receptor concept**, which grew from Langley's "receptive substance" and Ehrlich's "corpora non agunt nisi fixata" (agents do not act unless bound), still frames the field. Specific, saturable, stereoselective binding that is coupled to a response is the operational signature of a receptor.

**Target space.** Approved small molecules and biologics act on a surprisingly small fraction of the proteome, a few hundred human proteins out of roughly twenty thousand genes. GPCRs alone account for roughly a third of approved drugs, followed by ion channels, nuclear receptors, kinases and other enzymes. The concept of **druggability** asks whether a protein has a pocket that can bind a drug-like molecule with high affinity. Classical druggability is now widening through protein–protein interaction inhibitors, covalent ligands, allosteric modulators, targeted protein degraders and oligonucleotides, which act on RNA rather than protein.

**Classification problems.** Mechanistic, therapeutic and chemical classifications often disagree. "Antidepressant" groups drugs with different mechanisms (SERT inhibition, MAO inhibition, α2 antagonism). A single mechanism, such as calcineurin inhibition, can map to several therapeutic uses. The ATC system (Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical) layers anatomy, therapeutic use and chemistry in a hierarchy. Mechanism-based classification predicts class effects best, but it fails for **polypharmacology**: most CNS drugs bind several receptors, and their clinical profile is the sum of all those interactions.

**Stereochemistry matters.** Enantiomers can differ in affinity, efficacy, metabolism or toxicity. Single-enantiomer re-launches ("chiral switches") such as esomeprazole and escitalopram show that a "drug" is often a defined stereoisomer rather than a structure on paper.
levels.expert:
At the bedside, the question "what is this drug?" really means "what does it hit, what else does it hit, and how does the body handle it?" Senior clinicians think in **mechanism first**, because mechanism predicts both the benefit and the side-effect list. A pharmacist who sees "-olol" already expects bradycardia, masked hypoglycemic warning signs and bronchospasm risk in a patient with asthma.

**Naming pitfalls cause real harm.** Look-alike, sound-alike pairs are a classic error source: hydroxyzine and hydralazine, Celebrex and Celexa, and many others. Hospitals use "tall-man lettering" (hydrOXYzine vs hydrALAZINE) to reduce mix-ups. Always reconcile medications by **generic name**, because one patient can hold two bottles of the same drug under two brand names and accidentally take a double dose.

**Class effects are not guaranteed.** Drugs in one class usually share on-target effects, but off-target properties differ. Within beta blockers, carvedilol also blocks α1 receptors, and nebivolol releases nitric oxide. Within statins, lipophilicity and metabolic route (CYP3A4 for simvastatin and atorvastatin vs minimal CYP metabolism for rosuvastatin and pravastatin) change interaction risk.

**On-target vs off-target toxicity.** Some adverse effects are the mechanism itself, in the wrong tissue or at too high an exposure: bleeding with anticoagulants, hypoglycemia with insulin. Others come from a second target, like hERG channel blockade causing QT prolongation with many structurally unrelated drugs. Distinguishing the two tells you whether switching within the class will help. An on-target toxicity follows the whole class; an off-target one may not.

**Neurosurgical relevance.** In the operating room and ICU, a neurosurgeon handles agents from many classes at once: anesthetics, osmotic agents, antiseizure drugs, anticoagulants and their reversal agents. Thinking in targets keeps the list manageable.

keyPoints: A drug changes biological function, usually by binding a molecular target
Most targets are proteins: receptors, enzymes, ion channels, transporters
Every drug has a chemical, a generic (nonproprietary) and a brand name
Generic stems signal class: -olol, -pril, -sartan, -statin, -mab, -tinib
Pharmacokinetics = what the body does to the drug; pharmacodynamics = what the drug does to the body
Selectivity is always relative and concentration-dependent

test.q: Which best defines a drug's target?
choices: The organ where the drug is absorbed
The enzyme that metabolizes the drug
The specific molecule the drug binds to produce its effect
test.explain: The target is the molecule (usually a protein) whose binding produces the effect. Absorption sites, metabolizing enzymes and diseases are separate concepts.

test.q: A drug whose generic name ends in -pril is most likely:
test.explain: -pril is the WHO stem for ACE inhibitors (lisinopril, enalapril). -olol = beta blocker, -sartan = ARB, -statin = HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor.

test.q: Which statement about pharmacokinetics is correct?
choices: It only applies to intravenous drugs
It describes receptor binding and efficacy
It describes what the body does to the drug: absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion
It is the same as toxicology
test.explain: PK = what the body does to the drug (ADME). PD = what the drug does to the body.

test.q: Which drug acts WITHOUT binding a specific protein target?
choices: An antacid such as calcium carbonate
test.explain: Antacids neutralize stomach acid by a simple chemical reaction. Atenolol, omeprazole and lisinopril all bind specific proteins.

test.q: Ibuprofen is to Advil as:
choices: Generic name is to brand name
Brand name is to generic name
Chemical name is to generic name
test.explain: Ibuprofen is the generic (nonproprietary) name; Advil is a brand (proprietary) name.

test.q: Which name of a drug should be used when reconciling a patient's medications to avoid duplicates? (one word)
test.explain: The generic (nonproprietary) name identifies the active ingredient. One generic drug may be sold under many brand names, so reconciling by brand can hide duplicates.

test.q: Drugs with names ending in -mab are monoclonal ___.
test.explain: The -mab stem marks monoclonal antibodies (adalimumab, trastuzumab).

test.q: A molecule that binds to a receptor is called a:
test.explain: Any molecule that binds a receptor is a ligand. It may be an agonist (activates) or an antagonist (blocks).

test.q: Why is mechanism-based classification usually the most useful?
choices: Drugs sharing a target tend to share benefits and side effects
It is the easiest to memorize
test.explain: Drugs acting on the same target tend to share on-target effects, both therapeutic and adverse.

test.q: Pharmacodynamics describes what the ___ does to the body.
test.explain: PD = what the drug does to the body: binding, signaling, effect.

test.q: Bleeding caused by an anticoagulant is best described as:
test.explain: Bleeding is the anticoagulant mechanism itself, at too high an effect. That is on-target toxicity, so switching within the class does not remove it.

test.q: What does the stem -olol indicate? (two words)
test.explain: -olol marks β-adrenoceptor antagonists such as propranolol and metoprolol.

kidTest.q: A drug is like a key. What is the lock?
choices: A tiny spot on your cells
kidTest.explain: Drugs fit special spots on cells, like a key fits a lock.

kidTest.q: Which name is the company's name for a drug?
kidTest.explain: The brand name is the name a company puts on the box.

kidTest.q: Drugs in the same family usually:
kidTest.explain: Drug families share a way of working.

kidTest.q: Ibuprofen is a drug's:
kidTest.explain: Ibuprofen is the generic (real) name. Advil is a brand name.

kidTest.q: A drug fits a cell like a key fits a ___. (one word)
kidTest.explain: The key-and-lock picture shows how a drug fits its target.

advancedTest.q: Carvedilol and metoprolol are both beta blockers. Which property is unique to carvedilol among them?
advancedTest.explain: Carvedilol also blocks α1 receptors, adding vasodilation. Metoprolol is β1-selective. This is why class effects don't capture every property.

advancedTest.q: QT prolongation seen with many structurally unrelated drugs is most often due to:
advancedTest.explain: hERG blockade reduces IKr, delays repolarization and prolongs the QT interval. It is a classic off-target liability that crosses drug classes.

advancedTest.q: A single-enantiomer re-launch of a racemic drug is called:
advancedTest.explain: Esomeprazole (from omeprazole) and escitalopram (from citalopram) are chiral switches.

advancedTest.q: Name the hospital safety technique that writes look-alike drug names with partial capitals (e.g. hydrOXYzine). (two words)
advancedTest.explain: Tall-man lettering highlights the differing parts of look-alike names to reduce selection errors.

lessons.title: Ligand-Gated Ion Channels

levels.kid:
Some locks on your cells are also tiny doors. When the right chemical key fits, the door pops open in a blink, and little charged bits called ions rush through.

If positive ions rush in, the cell gets excited and sends a signal, like a doorbell ringing. If negative ions rush in, the cell calms down and stays quiet.

These fast doors help your muscles move and your brain think. Some medicines hold the door open a bit longer to calm the brain down. Others jam the door shut, so a muscle relaxes during surgery.
levels.hs:
A **ligand-gated ion channel** is a receptor that is also a channel. When a neurotransmitter binds, the protein changes shape and opens a pore through the cell membrane, and ions flow through within milliseconds. That makes these the **fastest** receptors in the body.

What the channel lets through decides the effect:
- **Na+ or Ca2+ entering** makes the inside of the cell more positive (depolarization), so the cell is more likely to fire. These are **excitatory**.
- **Cl− entering** makes the inside more negative (hyperpolarization), so the cell is less likely to fire. These are **inhibitory**.

Key examples:
- **Nicotinic acetylcholine receptor**: at the neuromuscular junction, ACh opens it and the muscle contracts. Neuromuscular blockers used in surgery block it.
- **GABA-A receptor**: the brain's main inhibitory receptor, a chloride channel. Benzodiazepines and many anesthetics make it work harder.
- **NMDA and AMPA receptors**: glutamate receptors that drive excitation, learning and memory.
- **5-HT3 receptor**: a serotonin-gated channel in the gut and brainstem. Ondansetron blocks it to stop vomiting.

Because these channels are so fast, drugs acting on them produce effects within seconds, which is why many anesthetics and muscle relaxants target them.
levels.college:
Ligand-gated ion channels (ionotropic receptors) couple agonist binding directly to the opening of an integral pore. Signaling occurs in milliseconds, with no second messenger.

**Families**
- **Cys-loop (pentameric) receptors**: five subunits around a central pore, each with four transmembrane segments (M1–M4); M2 lines the pore. The family includes nicotinic ACh receptors and 5-HT3 receptors (cation-selective) and GABA-A and glycine receptors (anion-selective).
- **Ionotropic glutamate receptors**: tetramers, namely AMPA, kainate and NMDA.
- **P2X receptors**: ATP-gated trimers.

**Nicotinic receptors.** The adult muscle receptor is (α1)2β1δε; the fetal form carries γ instead of ε. Two ACh molecules must bind (at α–δ and α–ε interfaces) to open the channel. Neuronal subtypes include α4β2 and homomeric α7.

**GABA-A receptors.** The common synaptic form is two α, two β and one γ2 subunit. GABA binds at β–α interfaces. Benzodiazepines bind a separate site at the α–γ2 interface and act as **positive allosteric modulators**: they increase the **frequency** of channel opening and require GABA to be present. Barbiturates increase the **duration** of opening and, at high concentrations, open the channel directly, which helps explain their lower safety margin. Propofol, etomidate, neurosteroids and volatile anesthetics also potentiate GABA-A.

**NMDA receptors** need glutamate plus a co-agonist (glycine or D-serine) and relief of a voltage-dependent **Mg2+ block** by depolarization. They are highly Ca2+-permeable, which makes them coincidence detectors for synaptic plasticity.

**5-HT3** is the only ionotropic serotonin receptor; ondansetron and other "-setrons" antagonize it.
levels.phd:
Ionotropic receptors convert chemical binding into conductance changes through allosteric coupling between the extracellular binding domain and a transmembrane gate several nanometers away. The **Monod–Wyman–Changeux** framework describes them well: the receptor exists in resting, open and desensitized states, and agonists stabilize the open state more than the resting one. Desensitization, a high-affinity closed state, shapes synaptic currents and explains how succinylcholine can produce a persistent block.

**Structure.** Cryo-EM structures of the Cys-loop family show an extracellular β-sandwich domain whose orthosteric site sits at subunit interfaces, capped by loop C. Agonist binding closes loop C, which twists the extracellular domain and tilts the M2 helices to open a hydrophobic gate near the middle of the pore. Ion selectivity is set by rings of charged residues at the pore's intracellular end; swapping a few of them can convert a cation channel into an anion channel.

**Subunit diversity creates pharmacology.** GABA-A receptors assemble from 19 known subunits. α1-containing receptors mediate sedation and anterograde amnesia; α2/α3 are linked to anxiolysis and muscle relaxation; α5 to cognition. Extrasynaptic δ-containing receptors produce tonic inhibition and are especially sensitive to neurosteroids; this is the rationale behind neurosteroid drugs for postpartum depression. Etomidate's action depends heavily on β2/β3 subunits (the β3 N265 residue is a classic determinant).

**Glutamate receptors.** The NMDA receptor's GluN2 subunit (2A–2D) determines its deactivation kinetics, Mg2+ sensitivity and pharmacology. Memantine's clinical tolerability, compared with other channel blockers, is attributed to fast off-rate and partial trapping kinetics, which let it block pathological tonic activation while sparing phasic synaptic transmission. AMPA receptor Ca2+ permeability depends on RNA editing of GluA2 at the Q/R site; unedited, Ca2+-permeable AMPA receptors contribute to excitotoxicity.

**Allosteric sites** in the transmembrane domain (anesthetics, neurosteroids) and at non-orthosteric interfaces (benzodiazepines) make these receptors ideal for modulators that refine rather than replace endogenous signaling.
levels.expert:
Ligand-gated channels are where anesthesia, neuromuscular blockade, seizure control and antiemesis converge, so the operating room is essentially applied ionotropic pharmacology.

**Neuromuscular junction.** Succinylcholine is a depolarizing agonist at nicotinic receptors. After denervation, burns, prolonged immobilization, stroke or spinal cord injury, the muscle membrane up-regulates extrajunctional receptors, including fetal γ-containing and α7 receptors. Succinylcholine then depolarizes a much larger area and can release enough potassium to cause **life-threatening hyperkalemia**. This is a real hazard in neurosurgical and trauma patients, typically starting a couple of days after the injury, and nondepolarizing blockers are preferred in these settings. Conversely, myasthenia gravis, with fewer functional receptors, produces resistance to succinylcholine and marked sensitivity to nondepolarizing agents.

**GABA-A in practice.** Benzodiazepines have a ceiling effect when used alone, but they act synergistically with opioids, alcohol and other GABAergic agents, and those combinations drive respiratory depression. Flumazenil competitively reverses the benzodiazepine site. It can precipitate seizures in benzodiazepine-dependent patients or after mixed overdoses (especially with tricyclics), so it is not a routine "coma cocktail" drug. In refractory status epilepticus, prolonged seizures internalize synaptic GABA-A receptors while NMDA receptors traffic to the membrane.

**Etomidate** preserves hemodynamics, which helps in the unstable patient, but it inhibits adrenal 11β-hydroxylase and suppresses cortisol synthesis.

**5-HT3 antagonists** are first-line for postoperative nausea, but they can prolong the QT interval; check the ECG and electrolytes in at-risk patients.

**Thinking pattern:** when a drug acts within seconds on excitability, think ionotropic. When it acts over minutes, think GPCR. Over hours to days, think gene transcription.

keyPoints: Ligand-gated ion channels open a pore when a ligand binds and act in milliseconds
Na+/Ca2+ influx excites; Cl− influx inhibits
Cys-loop family: nicotinic ACh, GABA-A, glycine, 5-HT3 (pentamers)
Benzodiazepines increase GABA-A opening frequency; barbiturates increase duration
NMDA receptors need glutamate, a co-agonist (glycine/D-serine) and relief of Mg2+ block
5-HT3 is the only ionotropic serotonin receptor (blocked by ondansetron)

test.q: What makes ligand-gated ion channels the fastest receptors?
choices: They are found only in muscle
Binding directly opens an ion pore
test.explain: Agonist binding opens the channel directly, so ions flow within milliseconds with no second messenger.

test.q: Opening of a chloride channel in a typical neuron usually causes:
test.explain: Cl− influx makes the membrane potential more negative (or clamps it near the Cl− reversal potential), which inhibits firing.

test.q: Which receptor is NOT a ligand-gated ion channel?
test.explain: β1-adrenergic receptors are GPCRs coupled to Gs. The others are ionotropic.

test.q: Benzodiazepines enhance GABA-A receptors by:
choices: Directly opening the channel without GABA
Increasing the frequency of channel opening
Increasing the duration of channel opening
test.explain: Benzodiazepines are positive allosteric modulators that increase opening frequency and need GABA present. Barbiturates increase duration and can open the channel directly at high concentrations.

test.q: Which drug blocks 5-HT3 receptors to prevent nausea and vomiting?
test.explain: Ondansetron is a 5-HT3 antagonist. Sumatriptan is a 5-HT1B/1D agonist; fluoxetine inhibits SERT.

test.q: At resting membrane potential, the NMDA receptor channel is blocked by ___ ions.
test.explain: A voltage-dependent Mg2+ block is relieved by depolarization, so NMDA receptors act as coincidence detectors.

test.q: Besides glutamate, the NMDA receptor needs a co-agonist: glycine or D-___.
test.explain: Glycine or D-serine binds the GluN1 subunit and is required for channel opening.

test.q: Neuromuscular blocking drugs used in surgery act at which receptor?
choices: Nicotinic acetylcholine receptor at the neuromuscular junction
test.explain: They act on muscle-type nicotinic receptors at the motor end plate.

test.q: How many subunits does a Cys-loop receptor such as GABA-A have?
test.explain: Cys-loop receptors are pentamers. Glutamate receptors are tetramers and P2X receptors are trimers.

test.q: Name the main inhibitory ligand-gated chloride channel in the brain. (e.g. XXXX-A)
test.explain: GABA-A is the principal fast inhibitory receptor in the brain.

test.q: Memantine acts on the NMDA receptor as:
test.explain: Memantine enters and blocks the open channel pore, so it acts most where the channel is overactive.

test.q: Which neurotransmitter opens the nicotinic receptor at the neuromuscular junction? (one word)
test.explain: Acetylcholine released from the motor nerve opens muscle nicotinic receptors.

kidTest.q: These special locks are also tiny:
kidTest.explain: Ligand-gated channels are like doors that open when the right key fits.

kidTest.q: How fast do these doors open?
kidTest.explain: They open in milliseconds, faster than a blink.

kidTest.q: If the door lets in calming bits, the cell gets:
kidTest.explain: Inhibitory channels calm the cell down.

kidTest.q: These fast doors help with:
kidTest.explain: They carry fast signals in nerves and muscles.

kidTest.q: Tiny charged bits that rush through the door are called ___.
kidTest.explain: Ions are tiny charged particles like sodium and chloride.

advancedTest.q: A patient with a spinal cord injury three weeks ago needs rapid sequence intubation. Why avoid succinylcholine?
choices: Upregulated extrajunctional nicotinic receptors can cause severe hyperkalemia
It causes malignant hyperthermia in all spinal patients
advancedTest.explain: Denervation up-regulates extrajunctional (including fetal γ and α7) receptors; succinylcholine depolarizes them broadly and releases a large potassium load.

advancedTest.q: Why can flumazenil be dangerous after a mixed overdose involving a tricyclic antidepressant?
choices: It may unmask seizures by removing benzodiazepine protection
It is a full GABA-A agonist
advancedTest.explain: Removing benzodiazepine effect can unmask the proconvulsant effect of the TCA (and precipitate withdrawal seizures in dependent patients).

advancedTest.q: Which mechanism helps explain benzodiazepine resistance in prolonged status epilepticus?
choices: Internalization of synaptic GABA-A receptors with surface trafficking of NMDA receptors
Loss of Mg2+ from the extracellular fluid
advancedTest.explain: Activity-dependent GABA-A internalization reduces benzodiazepine targets, while NMDA receptors increase, supporting early treatment and NMDA-directed options.

advancedTest.q: Etomidate's hemodynamic stability comes with which endocrine liability?
advancedTest.explain: Etomidate inhibits 11β-hydroxylase, suppressing cortisol synthesis.

lessons.title: G Protein-Coupled Receptors

levels.kid:
Some locks on your cells work like a doorbell with a messenger inside. When the key fits the lock outside the cell, the lock wiggles. That wiggle wakes up a helper inside the cell called a **G protein**.

The G protein runs off and tells other parts of the cell what to do. One message can turn into lots and lots of messages, like one person shouting and a whole crowd passing it on.

These locks are slower than the door-locks, but their messages are big and strong. Many medicines work on them, like medicines for asthma, allergies and the heart.
levels.hs:
**G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs)** are the largest family of drug targets; roughly a third of all approved drugs act on them. Each GPCR is one protein that snakes through the cell membrane **seven times**.

How they work:
1. A ligand (like adrenaline) binds the outside part of the receptor.
2. The receptor changes shape and activates a **G protein** on the inside.
3. The G protein swaps a molecule called GDP for **GTP** and becomes active.
4. The active G protein turns enzymes on or off, which changes the level of **second messengers** such as cAMP or calcium.

The three main G proteins to know:
- **Gs** stimulates adenylyl cyclase, so cAMP goes **up**. Example: β1 receptors in the heart, which increase heart rate.
- **Gi** inhibits adenylyl cyclase, so cAMP goes **down**. Example: μ-opioid receptors and α2 receptors.
- **Gq** activates phospholipase C, which releases **calcium** inside the cell. Example: α1 receptors that constrict blood vessels.

GPCR signaling takes seconds rather than milliseconds, but it is **amplified**: one receptor can activate many G proteins, and each enzyme makes many second-messenger molecules. That is why tiny amounts of a hormone can have big effects.
levels.college:
GPCRs are seven-transmembrane (7TM) receptors that act as guanine nucleotide exchange factors for heterotrimeric G proteins (Gα, Gβ, Gγ). The human genome encodes roughly 800 GPCRs, about half of them sensory (olfactory, taste).

**The G protein cycle.** An agonist stabilizes an active receptor conformation that catalyzes GDP release from Gα. GTP binds, and Gα-GTP separates from Gβγ; both then regulate effectors. Gα's intrinsic GTPase hydrolyzes GTP to GDP and ends the signal; **RGS proteins** speed up that hydrolysis.

**Major Gα families**
- **Gs**: activates adenylyl cyclase, raising cAMP and activating PKA. Receptors: β1, β2, β3, D1, H2, V2.
- **Gi/o**: inhibits adenylyl cyclase; Gβγ opens GIRK K+ channels and inhibits voltage-gated Ca2+ channels. Receptors: α2, M2, D2, μ/κ/δ opioid, GABA-B, 5-HT1.
- **Gq/11**: activates PLCβ, which cleaves PIP2 into IP3 (releases Ca2+ from the ER) and DAG (activates PKC). Receptors: α1, M1, M3, H1, V1, AT1, 5-HT2.
- **G12/13**: activates RhoGEFs and the Rho/ROCK pathway.

**Classes.** Class A (rhodopsin-like) holds most drug targets. Class B (secretin family) binds peptide hormones such as GLP-1 and PTH. Class C (glutamate family, including mGluRs, GABA-B and the calcium-sensing receptor) has a large extracellular "Venus flytrap" domain and works as a dimer.

**Regulation.** **GRKs** phosphorylate agonist-occupied receptors, and **β-arrestins** bind them. That uncouples the G protein (desensitization) and drives clathrin-mediated internalization. Receptors are then recycled or degraded (down-regulation). β-arrestins can also signal on their own.

Mnemonic for the classic autonomic receptors: "**qiss and qiq till you're siq of sqs**" lists α1 q, α2 i, β1 s, β2 s, M1 q, M2 i, M3 q, D1 s, D2 i, H1 q, H2 s, V1 q, V2 s.
levels.phd:
GPCRs are allosteric machines whose ligands shift an ensemble of conformations rather than flipping a single switch. The **extended ternary complex model** treats agonist, receptor and G protein as a linked equilibrium: receptors isomerize spontaneously between inactive (R) and active (R*) states, and the G protein itself stabilizes R* and raises agonist affinity. This explains **constitutive activity** and **inverse agonism**, as well as the classic "high-affinity state" seen in radioligand binding when G protein is present.

**Structural mechanism.** Crystal and cryo-EM structures, starting with the β2-adrenoceptor–Gs complex, show that activation involves an outward movement of transmembrane helix 6 of roughly 10–14 Å on the cytoplasmic side. This opens a cavity for the Gα C-terminal α5 helix. Conserved microswitches (the DRY motif "ionic lock" between TM3 and TM6, the NPxxY motif in TM7, the CWxP "toggle switch" in TM6, and a conserved sodium site in many class A receptors) couple the orthosteric pocket to the intracellular surface. Ballesteros–Weinstein numbering lets residues be compared across receptors.

**Functional selectivity.** Because different ligands stabilize different conformations, they can favor G protein or β-arrestin pathways, or one Gα subtype over another. This is **biased agonism**. Quantifying bias requires operational-model fits (transduction coefficients, Δlog(τ/KA)) against a reference agonist, and apparent bias can arise from system factors such as receptor reserve and assay amplification. The hypothesis that G protein-biased μ-opioid agonists would separate analgesia from respiratory depression has been challenged; low intrinsic efficacy may explain much of the observed profile.

**Allostery and location.** Allosteric modulators bind topographically distinct sites. They show probe dependence and a ceiling to their effect, and they can be more subtype-selective because allosteric sites are less conserved. Cinacalcet, a positive allosteric modulator of the calcium-sensing receptor, is the classic clinical example. GPCRs also signal from endosomes after internalization, and receptor dimerization (obligatory for class C) adds further complexity.
levels.expert:
Most of everyday clinical pharmacology is GPCR pharmacology: β blockers, β2 agonists, opioids, antipsychotics, antihistamines, triptans, antimuscarinics, angiotensin receptor blockers and GLP-1 agonists all act here.

**Desensitization is clinically visible.** Patients using a short-acting β2 agonist many times a day lose bronchodilator response as receptors are phosphorylated, uncoupled and internalized. Corticosteroids help partly by increasing β2 receptor transcription. Opioid tolerance similarly includes μ-receptor desensitization and adaptive changes downstream, such as adenylyl cyclase superactivation. Abrupt withdrawal then produces a rebound cAMP surge, which is part of the physiology of withdrawal.

**Up-regulation causes rebound.** Chronic antagonism increases receptor number. Stopping a β blocker abruptly in a patient with coronary disease exposes up-regulated β1 receptors to circulating catecholamines; tachycardia, angina or infarction can follow, so β blockers are tapered. Long-term D2 blockade is linked to receptor up-regulation and supersensitivity, a proposed contributor to tardive dyskinesia.

**Use the G protein to predict the effect.** Knowing the coupling lets you reason through unfamiliar drugs. α1 (Gq) agonists such as phenylephrine raise vascular Ca2+ and constrict vessels, producing reflex bradycardia. β2 (Gs) agonists raise cAMP in airway smooth muscle and relax it, and they also shift K+ into cells, which is why they treat hyperkalemia and can cause hypokalemia. V2 (Gs) signaling inserts aquaporin-2 water channels; vaptans block it to treat hyponatremia, and overly fast correction risks osmotic demyelination.

**Neurocritical relevance.** Vasopressors (α1, V1), sedation (α2 agonism with dexmedetomidine, which allows a more arousable state without major respiratory depression), and analgesia (μ agonists) are all GPCR choices made daily in the neuro-ICU. Receptor reasoning beats memorizing lists.

keyPoints: GPCRs have seven transmembrane helices and are the largest drug-target family
Agonist binding makes Gα exchange GDP for GTP; GTP hydrolysis ends the signal
Gs raises cAMP, Gi lowers cAMP (Gβγ opens GIRK), Gq activates PLC → IP3/Ca2+ and DAG/PKC
α1 Gq, α2 Gi, β1/β2 Gs, M1/M3 Gq, M2 Gi, D1 Gs, D2 Gi, H1 Gq, H2 Gs, V1 Gq, V2 Gs
GRKs and β-arrestins desensitize and internalize receptors
Biased agonists favor G protein or β-arrestin pathways

test.q: How many times does a GPCR cross the cell membrane?

test.explain: μ-opioid receptors couple to Gi/o: they lower cAMP, open GIRK channels and inhibit presynaptic Ca2+ channels.

test.explain: IP3 releases Ca2+ from the endoplasmic reticulum; DAG activates protein kinase C.

Signal amplification through G proteins and second messengers
The hormone is converted to a drug

kidTest.explain: Asthma inhalers act on β2 receptors, which are GPCRs.

choices: Up-regulation of β1 receptors exposed to catecholamines

The ligand blocking G protein synthesis

advancedTest.explain: Cinacalcet is a positive allosteric modulator (calcimimetic) of the class C calcium-sensing receptor, lowering PTH secretion.

Bias means the drug binds two receptors
Apparent bias must be quantified against a reference agonist because system amplification can distort it

lessons.title: Enzyme-Linked and Nuclear Receptors

levels.kid:
Some locks on the outside of a cell come in two halves. When a key fits, the two halves hug each other and start passing little "tags" back and forth. Those tags tell the cell to grow, use sugar or fight germs. Insulin works on a lock like this.

Other locks are hidden **inside** the cell, near the cell's instruction book, called DNA. Some keys are oily, so they slip right through the cell's wall to reach them. When the key fits, the lock opens a page in the instruction book, and the cell starts making new things. This is slow, like baking bread instead of making toast, but it lasts a long time.
levels.hs:
Two more receptor families finish the set.

**Enzyme-linked receptors** sit in the membrane. Their outside part binds the ligand, and their inside part is (or recruits) an **enzyme**, usually a **kinase** that adds phosphate groups to proteins. The most important type is the **receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK)**. When a growth factor or insulin binds, two receptor units come together and phosphorylate each other. Those phosphates act as docking sites that switch on pathways for growth, survival and metabolism. RTKs work over minutes to hours. Overactive RTKs drive some cancers, so drugs block them: trastuzumab is an antibody against HER2, and many "-tinib" drugs are small molecules that block kinase activity.

**Nuclear receptors** are inside the cell. Their ligands are fat-soluble, so they cross the membrane. Examples include cortisol, estrogen, testosterone, thyroid hormone and vitamin D. When the ligand binds, the receptor acts as a **transcription factor**: it binds DNA and turns specific genes on or off.

This is the slowest kind of signaling, taking hours to days, because new proteins must be made. It also lasts long after the drug is gone. That explains why corticosteroids don't stop inflammation instantly but have strong, long-lasting effects.
levels.college:
**Receptor tyrosine kinases** (insulin receptor, EGFR/HER family, VEGFR, PDGFR, KIT) have an extracellular ligand-binding domain, one transmembrane helix and an intracellular tyrosine kinase domain. Ligand binding promotes dimerization (the insulin receptor is a preformed disulfide-linked (αβ)2 that changes conformation instead) and **trans-autophosphorylation**. Phosphotyrosines recruit SH2- and PTB-domain proteins (Grb2, IRS-1, PI3K), which activate the **Ras–Raf–MEK–ERK** and **PI3K–Akt–mTOR** pathways.

**Cytokine receptors** (for interleukins, interferons, EPO and growth hormone) have no intrinsic kinase. They are bound to **Janus kinases (JAKs)**, which phosphorylate the receptor and recruit **STATs**. STATs dimerize and move to the nucleus. JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib, ruxolitinib) block this.

**Other enzyme-linked receptors**
- **Receptor serine/threonine kinases** (TGF-β, BMP) signal through SMAD proteins.
- **Receptor guanylyl cyclases** (natriuretic peptide receptor-A for ANP and BNP) make cGMP. The NO receptor, soluble guanylyl cyclase, is cytosolic.

**Nuclear receptors** are ligand-activated transcription factors with a DNA-binding domain (two zinc fingers), a ligand-binding domain and activation functions (AF-1, AF-2).
- **Type I** (steroid receptors: GR, MR, ER, PR, AR) sit in the cytoplasm bound to HSP90. The ligand releases the chaperone, and the receptor dimerizes, translocates and binds hormone response elements.
- **Type II** (TR, RAR, VDR, PPARs) heterodimerize with RXR and often sit on DNA already, bound to corepressors until the ligand arrives.

Drugs: glucocorticoids (GR), spironolactone (MR antagonist), tamoxifen and raloxifene (SERMs), levothyroxine (TR), thiazolidinediones (PPARγ agonists), fibrates (PPARα agonists) and retinoids (RAR). Effects take hours and persist after the drug falls, because they depend on mRNA and protein turnover.
levels.phd:
**Kinase-coupled receptors.** For most RTKs, ligand-induced dimerization brings kinase domains together so the activation loop of one is phosphorylated in trans, releasing autoinhibition. The EGFR is an elegant exception: activation depends on an **asymmetric dimer** in which one kinase's C-lobe allosterically activates the other's N-lobe, much like cyclin activating a CDK. Oncogenic mutations such as L858R and exon 19 deletions destabilize the inactive conformation, making mutant EGFR both constitutively active and more sensitive to ATP-competitive inhibitors. Resistance follows predictable structural logic. The T790M "gatekeeper" mutation raises ATP affinity, defeating first-generation drugs; osimertinib overcomes it by binding covalently to Cys797, and C797S then removes that anchor. Signal output is shaped by negative feedback (phosphatases, ERK-mediated SOS phosphorylation), receptor endocytosis and ubiquitination by Cbl. Pathway inhibition therefore often relieves feedback and reactivates upstream signaling, which is a recurring mechanism of adaptive resistance.

**Nuclear receptor allostery.** Ligand binding repositions **helix 12** of the ligand-binding domain. An agonist conformation forms the AF-2 groove that binds LxxLL motifs of coactivators (SRC/p160 family), which recruit histone acetyltransferases. An antagonist conformation occludes the groove or favors corepressors (NCoR, SMRT) that bring histone deacetylases. **Selective modulators** such as SERMs exploit the fact that coregulator availability differs by tissue: tamoxifen is an ER antagonist in breast but a partial agonist in endometrium and bone.

**Glucocorticoid mechanisms** illustrate the transactivation/transrepression distinction. GR dimers bind GREs to induce genes (anti-inflammatory proteins such as annexin A1, MKP-1, GILZ, as well as metabolic genes), while GR monomers tether to and repress NF-κB and AP-1. The early hope that "dissociated" ligands favoring transrepression would separate anti-inflammatory benefit from metabolic harm proved too simple, because some anti-inflammatory effects require transactivation. Non-genomic steroid effects, which occur within minutes through membrane receptors or cytosolic signaling, also exist but are less understood.
levels.expert:
**Corticosteroids in neurosurgery.** Dexamethasone reduces **vasogenic edema** around brain tumors and abscesses by tightening the leaky blood–brain barrier, often improving symptoms within a day or so. It does **not** help cytotoxic edema, and in traumatic brain injury the CRASH trial showed corticosteroids **increased** mortality, so they are not used for head injury. Before a biopsy for suspected primary CNS lymphoma, steroids are ideally held when it is safe to do so, because lymphoma cells can undergo apoptosis and the biopsy may become non-diagnostic. Long-term steroid use brings hyperglycemia, myopathy, infection risk, GI bleeding risk (especially combined with NSAIDs), psychiatric effects and hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal suppression. Abrupt withdrawal after prolonged courses risks adrenal crisis, so plans include tapering and stress-dose coverage.

**Targeted RTK therapy in neuro-oncology.** EGFR amplification and the EGFRvIII variant are common in glioblastoma, yet EGFR inhibitors have largely failed there. Reasons include poor blood–brain barrier penetration (efflux by P-gp and BCRP), intratumoral heterogeneity and pathway redundancy. Bevacizumab, an antibody that binds VEGF ligand rather than the receptor, reduces edema and contrast enhancement on MRI ("pseudoresponse") without clearly prolonging overall survival. Reading post-treatment imaging requires knowing that pharmacology.

**JAK inhibitors** carry warnings about serious infection, thrombosis and major cardiovascular events, so screening (for latent TB, hepatitis B, and thrombotic risk) matters before starting.

**Thyroid hormone** acts through nuclear receptors. That is why its full effect after a change in levothyroxine takes weeks to judge on labs (the long half-life of T4 compounds the transcriptional delay).

**A clinical rule of thumb:** if an effect develops over hours to weeks and lingers after levels fall, suspect a transcriptional mechanism. Plasma concentration alone will mislead you about its timing.

keyPoints: Receptor tyrosine kinases dimerize and trans-autophosphorylate, then signal via Ras–MAPK and PI3K–Akt
Cytokine receptors lack intrinsic kinase activity and use JAK–STAT
Natriuretic peptide receptors are membrane guanylyl cyclases (cGMP)
Nuclear receptors are ligand-activated transcription factors for lipophilic ligands
Type I steroid receptors are cytoplasmic with HSP90; type II (TR, VDR, RAR, PPAR) pair with RXR
Transcriptional effects start in hours and outlast drug levels

test.explain: The insulin receptor is an RTK. GR is nuclear, β2 is a GPCR and GABA-A is an ion channel.

They act by changing gene transcription and protein synthesis

test.explain: TZDs activate PPARγ (insulin sensitization). Fibrates activate PPARα.

test.explain: Trastuzumab is a monoclonal antibody against HER2.

test.explain: TR, VDR, RAR and PPARs heterodimerize with the retinoid X receptor (RXR).

test.q: What is the family name for JAK-activated transcription factors? (abbreviation)

test.explain: STATs are phosphorylated by JAKs, dimerize and enter the nucleus to change transcription.

kidTest.q: Where are some locks hidden?
kidTest.explain: Nuclear receptors are inside the cell.

kidTest.q: The inside locks open a page in the cell's:
kidTest.explain: They change which genes in DNA are used.

kidTest.q: Is this inside-lock signal fast or slow?
kidTest.explain: Changing genes is slow, like baking bread, but lasts a long time.

kidTest.explain: Insulin works on a receptor tyrosine kinase.

advancedTest.explain: Osimertinib forms a covalent bond with Cys797; the C797S mutation then confers resistance.

advancedTest.q: In a patient with suspected primary CNS lymphoma, why are corticosteroids ideally withheld before biopsy when safe?

Different ER genes in each tissue

lessons.title: Enzymes, Transporters and Other Drug Targets

levels.kid:
Not every drug works on a lock. Some drugs work on the body's tiny **workers**, called enzymes. Enzymes build and break things all day long. A drug can sit in an enzyme's hands so it can't do its job. Aspirin does this to the worker that makes pain and swelling chemicals.

Other drugs work on **pumps**. Pumps carry things in and out of cells, like a bucket brigade. Some medicines for the stomach turn off the acid pump.

And some drugs stop germs by breaking their tiny machines, without hurting ours. That is how many germ-fighting medicines work.
levels.hs:
Receptors are only part of the story. Drugs also act on:

**Enzymes.** Enzymes speed up chemical reactions. Blocking one lowers its product or raises its substrate.
- **Reversible inhibitors** bind and let go. Statins block HMG-CoA reductase, an enzyme in cholesterol production. ACE inhibitors block angiotensin-converting enzyme.
- **Irreversible inhibitors** bind permanently. Aspirin attaches an acetyl group to cyclooxygenase (COX). The effect lasts until the cell makes new enzyme, which is why aspirin's effect on platelets (which can't make new protein) lasts for their whole lifespan.

**Transporters and pumps.** These carry ions or molecules across membranes.
- SSRIs block the serotonin transporter (SERT), leaving more serotonin in the synapse.
- Proton pump inhibitors block the H+/K+-ATPase that makes stomach acid.
- Digoxin blocks the Na+/K+-ATPase in heart cells.
- Loop diuretics block a salt transporter (NKCC2) in the kidney.

**Voltage-gated ion channels.** Local anesthetics block sodium channels so nerves can't fire. Calcium channel blockers relax blood vessels.

**Other targets.** Some cancer drugs damage DNA or freeze microtubules. Many antibiotics hit bacterial structures our cells don't have, like the cell wall. Some drugs don't need a target at all: antacids simply neutralize acid.
levels.college:
**Enzyme inhibition.** In competitive inhibition, the inhibitor binds the active site; apparent Km rises, Vmax is unchanged, and high substrate overcomes it. Statins compete with HMG-CoA. In noncompetitive inhibition, Vmax falls and Km is unchanged. In uncompetitive inhibition, the inhibitor binds only the enzyme–substrate complex, so both fall. **Irreversible** inhibitors form covalent bonds: aspirin acetylates a serine in COX-1 (Ser530); organophosphates phosphorylate the active-site serine of acetylcholinesterase. **Mechanism-based ("suicide") inactivators** are turned into reactive species by the target itself: clavulanate inactivates β-lactamases, and selegiline irreversibly inhibits MAO-B. Recovery from irreversible inhibition depends on new enzyme synthesis, so the effect outlasts the drug's plasma half-life.

**Transporters**
- SLC family (secondary active): SERT, NET and DAT (monoamine reuptake), NKCC2 (furosemide), NCC (thiazides), SGLT2 (gliflozins).
- P-type ATPases (primary active): Na+/K+-ATPase (digoxin), H+/K+-ATPase (omeprazole, which is activated by acid and binds covalently).
- VMAT2 (vesicular monoamine transporter): reserpine and tetrabenazine.
- ABC efflux pumps such as P-glycoprotein are mostly drug-handling proteins rather than targets.

**Voltage-gated channels.** Na+ channels are targeted by local anesthetics, class I antiarrhythmics, phenytoin and carbamazepine, often with **use-dependent** block (preferring open or inactivated channels). L-type Ca2+ channels are targeted by dihydropyridines (vascular) and verapamil/diltiazem (cardiac). K+ channels include hERG (class III antiarrhythmics) and K-ATP channels, which sulfonylureas close in β cells.

**Other targets**
- Tubulin: colchicine and vinca alkaloids inhibit polymerization; taxanes stabilize microtubules.
- DNA: alkylating agents and platinum compounds cross-link it.
- Microbial targets: transpeptidases (β-lactams), the 30S and 50S ribosomal subunits, and ergosterol (amphotericin B).
- Soluble mediators: monoclonal antibodies neutralize ligands such as TNF-α (infliximab) and VEGF (bevacizumab).
- Physicochemical: antacids, osmotic diuretics (mannitol), chelators, bulk laxatives.
levels.phd:
**Kinetic thinking about inhibition.** Beyond equilibrium constants, residence time (1/koff) increasingly explains in vivo efficacy. A drug with a slow dissociation rate keeps occupying its target as plasma levels fall, separating pharmacodynamics from pharmacokinetics. Covalent inhibitors take this to its limit. Their potency is best described by kinact/KI rather than IC50, because inhibition grows with time. The modern resurgence of **targeted covalent inhibitors** (ibrutinib at BTK Cys481, osimertinib at EGFR Cys797, sotorasib at KRAS G12C Cys12) relies on a reversible recognition step that positions a mild electrophile, typically an acrylamide, next to a non-conserved cysteine. That improves selectivity and lowers the risk of idiosyncratic reactions compared with promiscuous electrophiles.

**Transition-state and substrate mimicry.** Enzymes bind the transition state far more tightly than the substrate, so transition-state analogues (oseltamivir carboxylate for neuraminidase, many protease inhibitors) achieve very high affinity. Prodrug strategies sometimes exploit the target itself: proton pump inhibitors are weak bases that accumulate in the acidic canaliculus of parietal cells, where acid converts them into a sulfenamide that forms disulfide bonds with cysteines on the H+/K+-ATPase. Activation requires actively secreting pumps, which is why PPIs work best taken before a meal.

**Transporters as conformational machines.** SLC transporters follow alternating-access mechanisms. SERT structures with bound SSRIs show the drug occupying the central substrate site and locking an outward-open state, while an allosteric vestibule site explains escitalopram's distinct kinetics. Inhibitor classes differ in which conformation they stabilize, with consequences for selectivity and residence.

**Use-dependence** in Na+ channel blockers follows the modulated-receptor and guarded-receptor hypotheses: drugs bind with higher affinity to open or inactivated states, so rapidly firing (epileptic, ischemic or arrhythmic) tissue is preferentially blocked. Lidocaine's fast kinetics make it a weak blocker at normal heart rates and an effective one in ischemic, depolarized tissue, which is the molecular basis of its class Ib profile.
levels.expert:
**Irreversible inhibitors outlast their half-life.** Aspirin's antiplatelet effect persists for the life of the platelet, so recovery depends on platelet turnover, which takes days. The same is true of clopidogrel, an irreversible P2Y12 receptor blocker (a receptor, not an enzyme, but the same logic applies). For elective neurosurgery, antiplatelet drugs are usually stopped several days beforehand when the clinical risk allows, and platelet transfusion has a limited and debated role after antiplatelet-associated intracranial hemorrhage (the PATCH trial found worse outcomes with platelet transfusion in spontaneous ICH on antiplatelets). Ticagrelor is reversible but has no simple antidote in routine use, and its effect wears off over a few days.

**Use-dependent Na+ channel block** explains why phenytoin, carbamazepine and lacosamide suppress high-frequency seizure firing while sparing normal activity. It also explains why local anesthetic toxicity first appears as CNS excitation (perioral numbness, tinnitus, seizures) before cardiovascular collapse. Bupivacaine binds cardiac Na+ channels tightly and dissociates slowly, making it especially cardiotoxic; lipid emulsion is the specific rescue therapy.

**Transporter targets carry predictable syndromes.** Too much serotonin reuptake blockade, especially combined with MAO inhibitors, linezolid or other serotonergic drugs, causes serotonin syndrome: clonus, hyperreflexia, hyperthermia and agitation. VMAT2 inhibitors deplete monoamines and can cause depression and parkinsonism; tetrabenazine and its relatives are used for Huntington chorea and tardive dyskinesia.

**Know whether the target is the ligand, the receptor or the kinase.** Bevacizumab binds the VEGF ligand; trastuzumab binds the HER2 receptor; tofacitinib blocks the intracellular kinase. Those distinctions determine pharmacokinetics (antibodies stay outside cells and last for weeks), toxicity (hypertension, proteinuria and impaired wound healing with VEGF blockade, which matters for surgical timing) and resistance.

keyPoints: Competitive enzyme inhibitors raise apparent Km; noncompetitive inhibitors lower Vmax
Irreversible inhibitors (aspirin, organophosphates, PPIs) act until new protein is made
Transporter targets: SERT (SSRIs), Na+/K+-ATPase (digoxin), H+/K+-ATPase (PPIs), NKCC2 (loop diuretics), SGLT2
Voltage-gated Na+ channel blockers show use-dependent block
Other targets: tubulin, DNA, microbial structures, soluble ligands (antibodies)
Some drugs act physicochemically: antacids, osmotic diuretics, chelators

test.explain: Statins competitively inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting step of cholesterol synthesis.

Aspirin irreversibly acetylates COX-1 and platelets cannot make new enzyme

test.q: SSRIs act by blocking:

kidTest.q: Enzymes are the body's tiny:
kidTest.explain: Enzymes are like workers that build and break things.

kidTest.q: Aspirin stops the worker that makes:
kidTest.explain: Aspirin blocks COX, which makes prostaglandins.

kidTest.q: A pump in a cell is like:

kidTest.q: Some stomach medicines turn off the:
kidTest.explain: Proton pump inhibitors turn off the stomach's acid pump.

kidTest.q: The body's tiny workers are called ___. (one word)
kidTest.explain: Enzymes speed up chemical reactions.

advancedTest.q: Why is lidocaine an effective antiarrhythmic in ischemic tissue but weak at normal heart rates?
choices: Fast binding/unbinding kinetics plus preferential binding to inactivated channels in depolarized tissue
It is metabolized only in ischemic tissue
It only binds open K+ channels
advancedTest.explain: Use- and voltage-dependent block with fast kinetics means lidocaine accumulates mainly in rapidly firing or depolarized tissue.

advancedTest.q: The potency of a targeted covalent inhibitor is best described by:
advancedTest.explain: Covalent inhibition is time-dependent; kinact/KI captures both recognition and the inactivation rate.

advancedTest.q: Why do proton pump inhibitors work best when taken before a meal?

They need acid in actively secreting parietal cells to be converted into their active form

advancedTest.q: Bupivacaine cardiotoxicity is especially severe because it:
choices: Binds cardiac Na+ channels tightly and dissociates slowly
advancedTest.explain: Slow dissociation causes cumulative block; lipid emulsion therapy is the specific rescue.
